description: We're a team of passionate first-year Computer Science students at Ateneo de Manila University.
summary: Orbital Architect 3D is a space mission design game where anyone, with no science background, can design a spacecraft, launch it, and fly a real mission to Earth orbit, the Moon, or Mars. Players choose a mission, build a spacecraft from eight parts that each trade weight, power, money, data, radio time and build time, pick one of nine real launch sites, set up NASA Deep Space Network radio dishes, and fly a real-time 3D flight through liftoff, stage separation and orbit. A friendly flight engineer, Kap, guides first-time players through a full mission, explains every trade-off in plain words, and shows the real formula behind each resource, from the rocket equation to battery life in Earth's shadow. The physics is real, in a scaled-down solar system: thrust-to-weight, orbital mechanics, drag, eclipses, downlink capacity, and Earth's spin (launching near the equator really helps). A mission score rewards efficient engineering: money left over, fuel to spare, and finishing ahead of schedule. Beginner mode uses plain words and an autopilot; Realistic mode shows full telemetry and lets players steer. It teaches what real mission teams live with: there is no perfect design, only trade-offs.
details: What it does: Orbital Architect 3D lets anyone design and fly a complete space mission in six steps. 1) Choose a mission: Orbit Earth, Space telescope, Land on the Moon, or Land on Mars. 2) Build the spacecraft from 8 parts (frame, power, battery, computer, steering, heat control, science tool, rocket); every part shows one clear upside and one trade-off, and Kap, the flight engineer, explains each choice or builds it for you. 3) Pick one of 9 real launch sites; Earth's spin gives an eastward boost that is strongest near the equator. 4) Set up NASA Deep Space Network radio dishes and a radio band fast enough to bring the science home. 5) Fly a real-time 3D launch: the swing arms pull away, the booster drops at stage separation, and the spacecraft reaches orbit and sends data home whenever a ground dish can see it. 6) Results: a plain-language report on mass, power, budget, data, comms and time, plus a mission score that rewards efficient engineering (money left over, fuel to spare, finishing ahead of schedule) and keeps your best scores. How it works: React, Three.js and TypeScript, fully in the browser. The flight simulation uses Velocity-Verlet orbital mechanics with Earth, Moon and Mars gravity, atmospheric drag, eclipses and battery drain, downlink limits and Earth's rotation, in a scaled-down solar system. The math comes from the team's Project TALA research notes (rocket equation, thrust-to-weight, Hohmann transfers). A live validator runs 30+ engineering checks while you build. Sound and music are generated live with the Web Audio API. Planet surfaces use real 8K maps. Benefits and impact: It is built for students with no science background. Kap's guided first flight teaches the whole loop in a few minutes, every resource light opens a short explanation with the real formula, and failed missions explain exactly why they failed and how to fix them. Beginner mode uses plain words and an autopilot; Realistic mode shows full telemetry and manual steering. The goal is the lesson real mission teams live with: there is no perfect design, only trade-offs. Use of SI: AI coding assistants helped write and debug code, generate the synthesized music and sound code, and edit text; all design decisions, testing and gameplay were directed and reviewed by the team.
